name: Ki-pokomo
confidence_why: The fixed: penultimate syllable rule rests on Würtz's hedged 1889 missionary sketch, whose own examples (ka-dsá-ri, kambádsi) already put the accent off the penult, whereas Philippson 1991 treats Pokomo as a lexical pitch accent language with at most one high syllable per word (first stem syllable, penult or final, or none) and only a length peak on the penult, and Nurse 2008 transcribes pairs such as hu-na-gúy-a 'we buy' against hú-na-guy-á 'we will buy' that differ by accent placement alone, so the better reading is lexical accent rather than fixed stress, although Philippson himself calls his Pokomo data thin and doubtful.

catalog_quote: Betonung. Was die Betonung betrifft, so kann man es als stehende Regel betrachten, dass beinahe alle Wörter in ihrer nackten Form, d. h. wenn sie nicht in Verbindung mit anderen Wörtern gebraucht werden, den Ton auf der vorletzten Silbe haben. In der Rede erleidet der Accent jedoch mancherlei Verschiebungen, z. B.: kú-dsa kommen. ni-ma-kúdsa ich bin gekommen. ni-ku-dsá-ni ich bin am kommen. ka-dsá-ri? wann kam er? kámba er sagte. kambádsi? was oder wie hat er gesagt?
sweep_summary: Single works with stress in the title, Philippson 1991 (542-pp Paris V thesis on tone and accent in East Bantu), was located as an open full text on the DDL Lyon site (http://www.ddl.cnrs.fr/Fulltext/philippson/these.pdf;theses.fr says 'accessible: non', SUDOC lists only the thesis and an ANRT microfiche), downloaded to, and read at every Pokomo mention (27 hits, 18 pages). It refines and effectively contradicts the catalog's 'fixed-unreviewed penult' coding from Würtz 1889: Pokomo is an accentual (n+1 scheme) language in which a single lexical H falls on the penult, the final, or the first stem syllable and some words have none (pp. 41-42, 81, 415-416, 469), the penult carries a length but not a pitch culmination (p. 483), and after a historical penult attraction the language developed a strict word accent unaffected by the phrase (pp. 495-496). Recommended reclassify: lexical pitch accent / restricted tone with penultimate length culmination, deciding source Philippson 1991 pp. 81, 483, 495-496 (supersedes Würtz 1889), with the caveat that Philippson's Pokomo data rest on Whiteley's 6-pp vocabulary list and his own notes and he calls the language poorly known. A thesis summary (Philippson 1998, Faits de langues 11-12) exists on Persée but its PDF is altcha-protected (low priority). Bibliographic records (theses.fr, SUDOC, IdRef, DDL page) saved alongside; was already exhausted; HAL, archive.

new_statements.quote: pokomo (groupe XVIII) : mahumbo, "entrailles"; mákwaɸa, "aisselles"; maʃóká, "haches". [...] Toutes ces langues peuvent, certes, s'analyser comme étant accentuelles, en ce que seule une syllabe est mise en valeur sur le plan prosodique (il n'y a que trois schèmes à chaque fois), mais la mise en rapport des schèmes réalisés et des syllabes accentuées sous-jacentes est évidemment problématique et réclame une analyse serrée, que nous entreprendrons au cours des chapitres qui suivent.
new_statements.translation: pokomo (group XVIII): mahumbo 'entrails'; mákwaɸa 'armpits'; maʃóká 'axes'. [...] All these languages can, certainly, be analysed as accentual, in that only one syllable is prosodically prominent (there are only three schemes each time), but relating the surface schemes to the underlying accented syllables is obviously problematic and demands a close analysis, which we shall undertake in the chapters that follow.
new_statements.citation: Philippson, Gérard. 1991. Tons et accent dans les langues bantu d'Afrique orientale: étude comparative typologique et diachronique. Thèse d'État, Université Paris V. p. 81 (Chapitre trois, commentary on Tableau II, the '(a) : 3' languages); see also pp. 41-42, 415-416, 469, 483, 495-496.
new_statements.reading: Pokomo is coded by Philippson as an accentual language with n+1 lexical schemes: one syllable per word may carry a lexical H (accent), some words carry none (mahumbo), and the accented syllable is not fixed -- first stem syllable (mákwaɸa), penult (ɲóka, mukóno, ŋkúku, mpémbe) or final (ɲumbá, ʃoká) -- with H-spreading to the penult being post-lexical. The penult has only a length culmination, not a pitch one (p. 483), and word accent is strict, unaffected by the phrase (pp. 495-496). This is not a fixed-penultimate stress system; the penultimate prominence Würtz 1889 heard is the demarcative penult lengthening plus the frequent penult H. The catalog's 'fixed penult' coding should become 'lexical pitch accent / restricted tone with penultimate length culmination' (consistent with the Nurse 2008 App. 2 present-vs-future accent contrast already held by the project). Caveats: Philippson's own Pokomo data are thin (Whiteley's 6-page list plus own notes) and he himself calls the language 'assez mal connu et par conséquent douteux' (p. 42); Upper vs Lower Pokomo is not distinguished.

(1) In mákwaɸa the H sits on the class-6 prefix ma- (antepenult of the word), not on the "first stem syllable"; the three nominal patterns on p. 81 are therefore: no H (mahumbo), H on the prefix/antepenult (mákwaɸa), H on penult+final (maʃóká = BH ʃoká of p. 415 with the post-lexical leftward doubling). new_statements.relation_note: Contradicts the catalog record 'Ki-pokomo: penultimate stress (fixed penult)': Philippson describes a lexical pitch accent/restricted-tone system in which the marked syllable is lexically placed (first stem syllable, penult or final) and some words have no accent at all; the penult has only a length culmination, not a pitch one. It agrees with the existing_statement already held for this language, which is a prior reading of the same thesis (p. 81) and already recommends reclassification to 'lexical pitch accent / restricted tone with penultimate length culmination'. 41, 483 and 496 (strict word accent, no phrase influence) and the p. 415 correspondence data, all consistent with that earlie…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Philippson classes Pokomo as an accentual (restricted-tone / pitch accent) language: a stem carries at most one marked syllable (a lexical H, his 'accent'), and some words carry none, giving n+1 lexical schemes. The marked syllable is not in a fixed position -- p. 81 gives three nominal schemes mahumbo 'entrails' (unaccented), mákwaɸa 'armpits' (first stem syllable), maʃóká 'axes' (final H); p. 415 gives ɲóka, mukóno (penult H), ɲumbá, ʃoká (final H), ŋkúku, mpémbe, mbéju (HH merged with HB, H on the penult). The penultimate syllable has only a length culmination, not a pitch one (p. 483, class c). Long verb stems show a diachronic 'attraction to the penult' (kuháɸíka 'to vomit', p. 496), and the doubling of a H leftwards onto the preceding syllable (kúóna ɲúmbá, p. 494) is post-lexical (p. 495). The accent is a strict word accent, unaffected by the phrase (p. 496); Pokomo shows no syntactic conditioning of prosody (p. 298).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed as such. The leftward double association of a H onto the preceding syllable (e.g. maʃóká, kúóna ɲúmbá) is described as post-lexical H-spreading, not as a secondary stress (pp. 494-495).
new_statements.exceptions: Philippson's own caveats: Pokomo is 'assez mal connu et par conséquent douteux' (p. 41), its data rest on Whiteley's 6-page 'Ki-Pokomu vocabulary list' ms plus his own notes (pp. 515, 525), and rare schemes may be missing from the data (p. 79). Proto-Bantu HH has merged with HB (p. 415-416). Upper vs Lower Pokomo is not distinguished.
new_statements.identity_note: Philippson's 'pokomo' is E71 in Guthrie's coding (his group XVIII, Sabaki; p. 72) with data from Whiteley's 'Ki-Pokomu vocabulary list' and his own notes; he does not distinguish Upper from Lower Pokomo. The held Nurse 2008 Appendix 2 page (not among this task's works) is explicitly Lower Kipokomo.

readall_conflicts: One disagreement, between the catalog and the only open source. The catalog codes Ki-pokomo as fixed penultimate stress (penultimate stress). Philippson 1991 (the sole work listed, and the same work behind the existing_statement) instead treats Pokomo as an accentual language with n+1 lexical schemes: at most one H-marked syllable per stem, lexically placed (first stem syllable / penult / final), some words unmarked, a strict word accent with no phrasal influence, and a penultimate culmination of length only, not of pitch (pp. 41, 81, 415, 483, 496). both contradict the catalog's fixed: penultimate syllable coding. Philippson himself flags the Pokomo data as thin and 'douteux' (p. 41), so the pitch accent reading rests on one sparse source (Whiteley's 6-page word list plus Philippson's own notes).

audit.recode_to: Keep penultimate as the default word accent, but expect to add a restricted/grammatical tone-or-accent qualifier (verb TAM distinguished by accent placement, e.g. Lower Pokomo present hu-na-gúy-a vs future hú-na-guy-á) once Nurse & Hinnebusch 1993 (Philippson addendum) is read; 'the exceptions statement: none-stated' and the the primary-stress rule's claim that all shifts are 'the penult rule re-applying' should not survive
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: confirmed verbatim on the page scan we hold (Würtz 1889 p. 163 'Betonung') and in the full-volume scanned; it is the article's only accent statement. (2) Deciding source: an 1889 29-pp missionary grammar sketch, impressionistic, hedged ('beinahe alle Wörter'; accent 'erleidet.. mancherlei Verschiebungen' in speech). Held modern items are silent (Ipu 1982 excludes stress/tone; Shume 2017 syllable structure only; Meinhof 1905 only notes possible 'Tonhöhen' pairs). Glottolog and the record itself point to two unheld authoritative treatments (Nurse & Hinnebusch 1993, 780 pp, with Philippson's tone addendum; Philippson 1991/92, 542 pp). (3) A copies we hold already refines the classification: Nurse 2008 App. 2 p. 27 gives Lower Pokomo hu-na-gúy-a 'we buy' vs hú-na-guy-á 'we will buy' -- accent placement, not segments, distinguishes present from future, so accent is not invariably penultimate
audit.second_reader_evidence: The quotation was checked again. opened (Würtz 1889, ZAS II p.163, 'Betonung'): the deciding quotation is there verbatim with all six examples (kú-dsa, ni-ma-kúdsa, ni-ku-dsá-ni, ka-dsá-ri?, kámba, kambádsi?), all penult. In the full-volume scanned, article = lines 38237-43440) a full-text search for stress/accent Beton|Accent|Ton auf|Tonh finds only this passage (article lines 365-370); no second accent statement. WÜRTZ'S OWN PARADIGMS (new page-level observation): rendered ZAS II p.179 (p.186) at 300 dpi. Sporadic accent marks in the ka- and dsa-(future)

tone.quote: 3. All the languages represented in this group are tone languages but none marks tone in their current orthography. Tone will therefore not be marked in non-technical text. [...] 2. TONES Except in Kiswahili, tone is important for distinguishing meaning between words in all the other languages in this group. However, marking tone will make the written texts very complex, and because meaning of words can easily be discerned from the context, tone will not be marked in non-technical texts.

tone.quote: - Nyankore (J1 13), Ganda (J 15), Haya (J 22), Jita/Ruri (J 25), Pokomo (E 71), Giryama (E 72), ... and Makua (P 31), have all dropped the contrast *–cv́cv́/*–cv́cv̀; the resulting pattern is sometimes –cv́cv̀ like in Ganda, Haya or Nilyamba, sometimes –cv́cv́, like in Shambaa or Bemba and sometimes a different pattern altogether. Examples2 : ... Pokomo máfuha yúlimi ŋkûku3 múkuyu ... [n. 3] A H tone which should appear on the prefix is replaced by a HL fall on the first stem syllable if the prefix happens not to be syllabic.

tone.quote: Les parlers traités ici sont suffisamment documentés pour permettre d'établir leurs systèmes phonologiques. Cependant il manque encore une analyse approfondie des systèmes prosodologiques des parlers mijikenda, pokomo et ilwana, où les phénomènes tonales et d'accentuation ont une fonction distinctive avec des règles très compliquées. Cependant, pour le but des la comparaison dialectométrique, il suffit de se baser sur les données phonologiques.
tone.translation: The varieties treated here are sufficiently documented to allow their phonological systems to be established. However, an in-depth analysis is still lacking of the prosodic systems of the Mijikenda, Pokomo and Ilwana varieties, where tonal and accentual phenomena have a distinctive function with very complicated rules. However, for the purpose of dialectometric comparison it suffices to rely on the (segmental) phonological data.
